demo.title: Build two reasoning flows and compare their geometry
demo.caption: Pick a logic, topic and language for each flow. The trajectories are illustrative 2-D paths, but position, velocity and curvature similarity are computed with the paper’s own formulas. Press Play to draw each flow step by step.

story.title: Similar meanings can obscure similar reasoning
paragraphs: An argument’s representation mixes topic, language, entities and logical structure. Two English passages about weather can sit close together even when their deductions differ, while one deduction in two languages can sit far apart, so comparing isolated embeddings risks measuring surface content.

Take “If it rains, the ground is wet; it rains; therefore the ground is wet.” Replacing weather with servers (“If a server is overloaded, latency rises; …”) changes the concepts but keeps the inference. The paper applies this controlled variation to longer natural-deduction structures across topics and languages.

mechanism.title: Measure how a trajectory changes from step to step
paragraphs: Each reasoning step is represented by the average of its token representations at the final transformer layer, so a trajectory follows successive text steps at one layer, not one token through successive layers.

Position is where a step is embedded, velocity is the difference between neighboring steps, and curvature is the Menger curvature of three consecutive points, which measures how sharply the path turns. Position and velocity are compared by cosine similarity, curvature by Pearson correlation. Differences reduce the weight of components shared across a passage, such as its language or topic.

The theory treats the steps as samples from a continuous curve on which logical statements act as local controllers of velocity. It therefore predicts shared geometry for the same logic under different semantic carriers, which the experiment tests by grouping flows by logic, topic and language.

evidence.title: Positions group by language; velocity and curvature group by logic
paragraphs: Position similarity is highest for flows that share a language; velocity and curvature similarity are highest for flows that share logic. Randomly permuting the logical steps keeps the same sentences but collapses velocity and curvature similarity, while position similarity stays high: the logical signal lies in the order of the steps.
The pattern holds across six models (Qwen1.5-0.5B, Qwen2-0.5B, Qwen3 at 0.6B, 1.7B and 4B, and LLaMA3-8B) and changes little with model size or family.
